questions.prompt: In the practice this course teaches for ServiceNow architecture decisions, what is an Architecture Decision Record (ADR)?
options: A structured, written record that captures a significant decision's context, the real options considered, the decision made, and its consequences
A ServiceNow configuration item (CI) in the CMDB representing a design document
A change request record requiring CAB approval before a decision can be implemented
An automatically generated log of every field added to a table during a project
A dashboard widget showing Instance Health metrics for the current release
questions.explain: An ADR names the context that made a decision necessary, lists the real alternatives considered (including rejected ones), and records the decision and its consequences -- an industry-wide documentation practice, not a ServiceNow-specific feature.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B treats the ADR as a ServiceNow data record -- a CI tracked in the CMDB -- but an ADR is a plain written documentation artifact capturing reasoning, not any kind of ServiceNow table record or configuration item.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 1, the real boundary separating an architect-level decision from an admin or developer decision is ________ -- not difficulty or seniority.
questions.explain: Lesson 1 is explicit that the boundary isn't difficulty -- it's consequence and reversibility: decisions that are expensive or impossible to reverse once teams have built on top of them are architect-level, regardless of how technically hard the work is.

questions.prompt: A developer proposes using IntegrationHub for one new integration to a payroll vendor, local to that integration only. Per Lesson 1's framework, what would have to change about this choice for it to become an architect-level decision instead of a developer decision?
options: It's an admin decision, because routine integration pattern choices are always configured by admins
If the choice became a mandatory pattern every future integration on the platform had to follow, making it expensive to reverse across many integrations
If a more senior developer made the same choice instead
If the integration took longer than two weeks to build
questions.explain: A locally-scoped technical choice is a developer decision; it becomes architectural once it's generalized into a platform-wide standard that every future integration must follow, because reversing it then means re-touching every integration built under the old rule.

questions.prompt: A multinational retailer's EU subsidiary must, under a regional data-protection law, physically store certain personal data only within EU infrastructure -- not merely restrict access to it from outside the EU. Per Lesson 4, what does this fact imply for instance strategy?
options: Domain Separation always satisfies any data-residency law, since it logically isolates data per domain
A second production instance is never justified regardless of the law, since ServiceNow guidance always favors one instance

It is a genuine data-residency requirement -- if the company's existing instance's region can't satisfy it, a second regional production instance is justified, since logical separation inside one instance doesn't relocate underlying storage
The law is irrelevant to instance strategy because it only concerns application-level access control
questions.explain: Domain Separation partitions data logically within one instance; it doesn't relocate the underlying storage to a different region. A real physical-residency requirement that the existing instance's region can't satisfy is one of the two legitimate reasons a second production instance becomes the right call.

questions.prompt: Match each term from the Platform Architecture chapter to its real meaning.
right: The hidden field on every record that determines which domain it belongs to
Data visible and editable from a domain and all of its subordinate domains
Depending on a specific published version of another scoped application, instead of always-latest
The line deciding which tables, scripts, and features belong inside one scoped application vs. another
questions.explain: sys_domain is the hidden field driving Domain Separation's visibility rules; domain-extendable data is visible/editable from above; dependency pinning protects a consumer from a breaking change in a depended-on scoped app; a scope boundary should track a real functional and ownership line, per Lesson 6.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Domain Separation, per Lesson 5.
options: It exists for genuinely structural cases: separate subsidiaries under one parent, or an MSP serving distinct clients
Once enabled, every future script, report, and integration on the instance has to be written with domain awareness in mind
It should be adopted by default whenever an organization has more than one department
A GlideRecord query tested from the top domain will behave identically for a user in a subordinate domain
Every record in a domain-separated instance carries a hidden sys_domain field
questions.explain: Domain Separation is built for genuinely structural separation, not a generic multi-department default, and it adds a permanent domain-awareness cost to every future script -- a query that looks correct from the top domain can silently misbehave for a subordinate-domain user.

questions.prompt: Per the Platform Architecture Lab (Lesson 7), put these three architectural decisions in the order a Technical Architect should actually make them for a new acquisition with a data-residency constraint.
items: Confirm whether a data-residency law or genuine business-unit independence forces a second production instance
Decide whether Domain Separation is needed within each resulting instance
Draw scope boundaries for new scoped applications based on real team ownership
questions.explain: Instance strategy is decided first because a residency constraint can't be satisfied logically; Domain Separation is evaluated second, within whichever instance(s) result; scope boundaries are decided last, based on team ownership, independent of which instance the resulting apps live on.

questions.prompt: A team wants to add 18 new fields to the base `task` table to support a new process, rather than creating a new extended table. Per Lesson 8, what is the strongest architectural concern with this choice, even if each individual field looks harmless on its own?
options: ServiceNow technically limits any table to 40 fields total

Every added field permanently widens task and every table extended from it, increasing I/O per row and index-maintenance overhead for every future query and write -- regardless of whether this specific process needs most of those 18 fields
Extending task instead of building a new table always breaks existing SLAs automatically
Adding fields to task requires a new scoped application to be created first
questions.explain: Table width isn't free: every indexed or unindexed field adds data every query has to read and every write has to maintain, forever, on task and every table that extends it -- not just on the 18 new fields' own queries.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 9, archiving or deleting data before a required retention period has elapsed is a ________ problem, not merely a performance one.
questions.explain: Lesson 9 is explicit: confirm any archiving criteria against real compliance or legal retention requirements first -- a policy that archives or deletes data too early is a compliance problem, not a performance win.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about why CMDB/CSDM data quality degrades over time at enterprise scale, per Lesson 10.
options: Inconsistent classification happens when different teams invent slightly different patterns for functionally the same thing
Stale relationships persist when a decommissioned CI's link to a Business Service is never removed because removing it wasn't anyone's assigned job
CMDB data quality holds steady by default once the model is correctly designed at launch
Orphaned or duplicate CIs can appear when Discovery and manual creation both populate the CMDB without a reconciliation process
Silent scope creep is prevented automatically by ServiceNow's platform architecture, with no governance process required
questions.explain: CMDB quality erodes gradually and predictably unless something actively pushes back against it -- inconsistent classification, stale relationships, and orphaned/duplicate CIs are three of the real mechanisms Lesson 10 names. It does not hold steady on its own, and scope creep is a governance problem, not something the platform prevents by itself.

questions.prompt: In ServiceNow integration architecture, what is the fundamental difference between a request-response integration and an event-driven integration?
options: Request-response has the calling transaction wait synchronously for an answer before continuing; event-driven publishes an event and lets the publisher move on without waiting for any subscriber
Request-response can only be built with IntegrationHub, while event-driven can only be built with a raw REST Message
Event-driven integration guarantees an event is always processed exactly once, with no possibility of duplicate delivery
Request-response is always asynchronous, while event-driven always blocks the calling transaction until a subscriber responds
Event-driven integration eliminates the need for any authentication between systems
questions.explain: Request-response couples the caller's performance to the external system's performance because it waits for a response; event-driven decouples them because the publisher fires the event and continues, with subscribers acting independently whenever they're ready.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C sounds like a real design goal, but Lesson 13 is explicit that event-driven systems have to deliberately design for the possibility of duplicate delivery (idempotency) -- exactly-once processing is a hard problem the pattern raises, not something it guarantees automatically.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a maintained record of every integration touching the instance -- external system, direction, pattern, authentication, and owner -- is called an integration ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 12 calls this artifact an integration inventory (sometimes called an integration catalog) -- without it, the question of what's actually integrated with an instance is answerable only by interviewing every team that's ever touched the platform.

questions.prompt: Per the Integration Architecture Lab (Lesson 14), put these steps in the order the technical architect actually took to bring order to the 12 ungoverned HR integrations.
items: Interview every team and inspect configurations to build a complete integration inventory
Set a single OAuth authentication standard, migrating the unrotated API-key integrations first
Evaluate the highest-volume integration (new-hire sync) for a move from request-response to event-driven
questions.explain: The architect first found out what actually existed (the inventory), then consolidated authentication onto one standard with the highest security risk migrated first, and only then re-evaluated integration pattern for the one integration whose volume had genuinely outgrown request-response.

questions.prompt: A new scoped-application team asks a Technical Architect to approve a custom role called billing_special_access with no documented naming convention behind it. Per Lesson 15, what is the real architectural gap this request exposes?
options: The role name is too long for ServiceNow's role field to store
Custom roles are never permitted on any scoped application regardless of naming
There's no standing role-naming convention and review standard in place, so each team invents its own ad hoc role rather than following a shared, self-documenting strategy
The request should be approved automatically since only the architect needs to understand the name
questions.explain: A Technical Architect's job is setting the standing role/ACL strategy -- a naming convention and a rule for when a new role is justified -- so a request like this is self-evidently wrong against an existing policy, rather than requiring a one-off judgment call each time.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 16, select every real workaround that overly restrictive security can drive users toward, each one less secure than the control it replaced.
options: Shared credentials, where a team shares one login to avoid a slow approval chain, destroying individual audit accountability
Shadow exports, where a user exports what they can see to an ungoverned personal spreadsheet
Shadow IT, where a team stands up its own unofficial tool outside the governed platform
Automatically escalating their own role to administrator without approval
Filing a formal exception request through the architecture review board
questions.explain: Lesson 16 names exactly three workarounds -- shared credentials, shadow exports, and shadow IT -- each caused by friction, not malice, and each strictly less secure than the control it was built to get around. Self-escalating a role isn't a named pattern here, and a formal exception request is the compliant path, not a workaround.

questions.prompt: Match each Security Architecture Lab decision to what it actually accomplished for the expense_line_item table.
left: Leaving the approval-chain-override field under finance_admin
Disabling the weekly full-table export job
Checking back after 2-3 weeks for new export requests
right: Granted the four frequently-needed, non-sensitive fields without exposing the one genuinely sensitive field
Kept the single genuinely sensitive field -- the one auditing bypassed approvals -- tightly controlled
Removed the actual mechanism that had been generating the ungoverned spreadsheet
Verified the workaround actually stopped, rather than assuming the fix worked because it shipped
questions.explain: Each step targets a different part of the real problem: a scoped role fixes daily access, the unchanged override-field ACL preserves genuine sensitivity, disabling the export job removes the workaround's source, and the follow-up check confirms the fix actually held rather than just shipping.

questions.prompt: A developer asks why the architecture review board bothers with code-review checklists for GlideRecord anti-patterns when the platform already has a Script Performance Profiler that can catch slow scripts. Per Lesson 18, what is the real answer?
options: The Script Performance Profiler cannot detect GlideRecord anti-patterns at all
The profiler is reactive -- it only finds a problem once it's already live and already slow; a code-review standard catches the same anti-pattern before it ever reaches a customer-facing instance
Code review checklists are only useful during the first year after go-live
There is no real difference; both approaches catch the problem at the same point in the lifecycle
questions.explain: Diagnostic tooling like the Script Performance Profiler is inherently reactive -- something is already degraded before it finds the cause. A code-review standard is proactive: it catches the same anti-pattern before merge, which is cheaper than any production fix.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 19, capacity planning tracks two independent dimensions of growth -- ________ growth, which strains node capacity and semaphore pools, and data growth, which strains query performance and storage.
questions.explain: User growth (more employees, more concurrent sessions) strains node and semaphore capacity directly; data growth (more records, more attachments) strains query performance and storage -- a rollout can move either dimension independently of the other.

questions.prompt: Per the Performance Architecture Lab (Lesson 20), put these three steps of the readiness assessment in the order the architect actually performed them.
items: Review the core table's indexing against the projected 3x data volume
Evaluate semaphore pool and scheduled-job headroom against 3x concurrent usage
Establish growth-tracking metrics and a monthly review cadence for the rollout
questions.explain: The architect checked table/index design against the data-volume projection first, then checked semaphore and scheduled-job capacity against the concurrency projection, and finished with a tracking plan to catch a wrong assumption during the actual rollout.

questions.prompt: Ahead of a platform upgrade, a scoped application is heavily used by hundreds of service desk agents daily and relies on an API ServiceNow's release notes flag as deprecated. A rarely-used UI Policy on an obscure form has no such dependency. Per Lesson 21, which gets tested against the pre-upgrade sandbox first, and why?
options: The rarely-used UI Policy, because simpler items should always be cleared out of the way first
Both should receive identical testing rigor regardless of usage or dependency risk
Neither needs sandbox testing if the current production behavior looks fine today

The heavily-used, deprecated-API-dependent application, because both its blast radius and its likelihood of breaking are high, and testing it first leaves maximum runway to fix a real blocker before the upgrade date
questions.explain: Upgrade triage prioritizes by blast radius and likelihood of breaking, not by how simple an item is. Testing the highest-risk item first leaves the most time to fix a real blocker; finding it in the final week leaves no time to respond.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Platform Lifecycle & Release Management to its real meaning.
right: A defined period before an upgrade's testing window when only critical fixes are released
Accumulated shortcuts and compromises that make future changes harder and riskier than they should be
Code built on a platform capability ServiceNow is phasing out, growing riskier with each release cycle it survives
A named, documented decision point confirming a production upgrade should proceed, based on sandbox results
questions.explain: A change freeze keeps the upgrade-testing baseline stable; technical debt is shortcuts that compound cost over time; deprecated-API reliance is one concrete source of that debt; and a go/no-go decision is the named checkpoint that turns sandbox results into a real production decision.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 21, put these upgrade-timeline milestones in the order they should actually happen before a production upgrade.
items: Communicate the target upgrade window to application owners and business stakeholders, months out
Upgrade the pre-upgrade sandbox and begin high-risk-tier testing, weeks out
Run the lighter-touch, low-risk-tier validation pass and make a documented go/no-go decision, in the final week
Perform the production upgrade in the communicated maintenance window, with high-risk customization owners on standby
questions.explain: Skipping the months-out communication step is the single most common upgrade-planning failure Lesson 21 names: technical readiness without stakeholder communication still produces a surprise, just a well-tested one.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 23, the strongest argument for prioritizing a specific piece of technical-debt remediation is usually that it is currently ________ a feature the business actually wants -- not simply that the code is old.
questions.explain: Lesson 23 says the strongest case reframes debt remediation as the thing standing between the organization and a feature it wants, rather than a competing priority against new feature work.

questions.prompt: A fast-growing organization's single platform team has a six-week backlog of department change requests, all routed through one central review queue. Per Lesson 25, what does this symptom most directly suggest?
options: A six-week backlog is normal and requires no architectural response

The organization has likely outgrown pure centralized governance and should consider moving toward federated governance with real guardrails (naming conventions, mandatory code review, a shared component library) rather than simply adding reviewers
The organization should immediately enable Domain Separation to give each department its own queue
The fix is to remove code review entirely so departments can ship faster
questions.explain: A backlog growing with demand is centralized governance's real downside at scale. Lesson 25's alternative is federated governance -- but only survivable with real guardrails in place, not simply removing central review.

questions.prompt: Select every real guardrail Lesson 25 says is required to make federated governance survivable at enterprise scale.
options: Naming conventions enforced consistently enough that tables, roles, and fields are recognizable across departments
Mandatory code review standards, so a department's own developer's work is still checked against platform-wide practice
A shared component library, so departments reuse the same vetted building blocks instead of each inventing its own
Removing all central oversight so every department can move at maximum speed
Giving one department permanent veto power over every other department's releases
questions.explain: Lesson 25 names three real guardrails -- naming conventions, mandatory code review, and a shared component library. Without them, federated governance isn't governance at all, just no governance with extra departments; neither removing all oversight nor giving one department veto power is part of that design.

questions.prompt: Per the Governance Lab (Lesson 28), put these four steps of rolling out the Employee Service Center to Finance and Marketing in the order the architect actually took them.
items: Choose federated governance with shared guardrails over centralized review for Finance and Marketing's genuinely different approval needs
Pilot the rollout with Marketing, the department with the simplest, most contained use case
Build the shared base request-intake experience once, with approval routing as a department-specific extension
Present the tradeoff to the CFO and department heads in cost, risk, and timeline terms
questions.explain: The governance model is chosen first because it shapes everything downstream; the pilot is sequenced by contained risk, not funding size; the shared-vs-specific line is drawn once the model and pilot are set; and the executive translation closes the loop so the decision actually survives contact with budget authority.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Governance & Multi-Department Implementation Strategy to its real meaning.
right: The first department to adopt a new capability, chosen for a clear and contained use case, not organizational importance
Functionality built once because every department needs it in essentially the same shape
Functionality built as an extension because one department's need is genuinely different, not just differently preferred
Presenting the same real tradeoff in cost, risk, and timeline terms a budget-holding audience can evaluate
questions.explain: These four terms are how Lessons 26 and 27 turn a multi-department rollout into a real, defensible plan: a contained pilot builds confidence, the shared/specific line keeps the base maintainable, and executive framing is what gets the plan actually funded.

questions.prompt: Meridian Health Network's board asks why Lakeshore Regional Health and Prairie View Health Partners can't each keep their own ServiceNow instance, since they're used to running independently. Using Chapter 2's actual test, what is the correct response?
options: A second instance is justified because Lakeshore and Prairie View use different legacy HR systems

Historical autonomy is a cultural and governance fact, not a technical one -- Meridian fails both legitimate justifications for a second production instance, since there's no data-residency requirement and no genuine business-unit independence (the systems will increasingly share patients, HR/finance functions, and executive reporting)
Yes, three separate instances should be built immediately, since each hospital system has always run independently
The decision should be based on which hospital system has the most IT staff
questions.explain: Chapter 2's test for a second production instance requires a genuine data-residency law or true business-unit independence. Meridian has neither: all three systems operate under the same regulatory jurisdiction and are consolidating precisely because they'll increasingly share data, which is the opposite of independence.

questions.prompt: Match each part of Meridian's HR data flow to the integration pattern and technology Lesson 30 actually assigns it.
left: An HR rep needing a live department/location confirmation to route a case
right: Event-driven sync via an IntegrationHub spoke, since nobody is waiting on an immediate answer
A custom Scripted REST integration
A MID Server-based integration pulling from a scheduled data extract, since it has no real modern API surface
A request-response lookup, since the rep is waiting right now for an answer before they can continue
questions.explain: Lesson 30 matches each HR data flow to the pattern that fits its real need: Workday's connector pattern supports an asynchronous IntegrationHub spoke, ADP needs a custom Scripted REST integration, Prairie View's aging system needs a MID Server batch pull, and a rep waiting on a live answer is exactly the case request-response exists for.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement a strong CTA-style defense of Meridian's architecture would make, per Lesson 32.
options: Three separate instances would mean paying the upgrade, security, and integration-endpoint maintenance multiplier three times over, indefinitely
A fourth hospital system joining later is a bounded, known pattern -- adding a subordinate domain -- though each additional domain adds testing overhead that compounds
Every integration in the architecture should be made event-driven for consistency, since event-driven is categorically more scalable
Locking the entire platform down at the same strict level as the regulated zone would be the correct response to a compliance concern
The regulated zone gets strict, audited controls specifically because that's where real risk justifies the friction -- not because the whole platform needs uniform maximum restriction
questions.explain: A strong defense names the real multi-instance cost, scales domains honestly (cheaper than more instances, but not free), and holds the line that uniform maximum security produces worse outcomes than risk-proportionate controls. Forcing consistency onto integration pattern choice, or locking down the whole platform, are exactly the overcorrections Lesson 32 warns a panel will probe for.
